thesis: As with printing, railroads and the transistor, the people who invent and build machine intelligence (labs, hyperscalers, chip and compute suppliers, which the authors call Genesis) will not keep most of the wealth it creates, because any released model is copied or distilled within months and its unit price falls toward the cost of compute, with Chinese open-weight models setting the floor. Genesis will keep spending anyway, because falling behind the frontier is fatal for each firm and because US growth, stock prices and retirement savings now ride on AI capex, so Washington will backstop it with Treasury, Fed and retirement money and will quietly take control of frontier labs, walling off a sovereign frontier that is no longer for sale. The durable gains will go to whoever owns the scarce, controllable crossings that intelligence must pass through to reach economic use, chiefly distribution networks with population-scale installed bases and the dollar itself as it spreads abroad through stablecoins and their carriers, and not to those who sell intelligence. Labor leaves the firm (offshore back offices first, then young entrants, while licensed US workers are shielded), firms shrink to a few operators paid like capital, the K-shaped split widens, and investors must sell the last era's Heights and buy the new ones before the market prices them.

definitions.chokepoint: The paper defines a Commanding Height as a scarce, controllable position of economic power whose holder durably captures the gains of increasingly capable and widely diffused intelligence. It sets the terms on which intelligence becomes economic activity, and unlike a passing bottleneck it takes a share of the activity it enables, so growth in that activity entrenches it further; its cash flows can multiply without its valuation rising. Criteria it uses (Part VI Margin, Part IV Constant Currency, Part VIII): (1) scarcity is necessary but not enough, since scarcity only shows a margin exists in principle; (2) durability: there is no cheap next-best route, whereas passing scarcities (power, then transmission, then chips) draw capital in and get competed away; (3) control: the nature of ownership, contract length and terms decide whether the position holds; (4) the political test of last resort: who else can claim the rent (regulators, ratepayer advocates, local opposition, antitrust, the sovereign), with very high margins inviting state action; (5) revenue that grows with the nominal value of activity flowing through it without matching capital spending, which also protects against inflation; (6) model-agnostic: the owner does not care which model wins; (7) a toll every participant in the era must pay, used more as the era grows. Its examples: rails of diffusion such as a global messaging app (WhatsApp) and the owner of the digital distribution network; the Neo-Dollar (USDT, its carriers, issuer reserve income); a population-scale installed base or everything apps (plural); licensed guilds (Fitch). Historical Heights: Standard Oil's pipelines, railroads, AT&T, Google Ads and Alphabet search, dominant local newspapers. The sovereign keeps a claim on gains wherever they land.
definitions.unit_seller: The paper does not use the term unit seller; the matching idea is Genesis, the industry that designs, trains, evaluates, hosts and serves models (labs, hyperscalers, neoclouds, chip suppliers) and sells the output as subscriptions and metered API tokens. Why it says they do not durably capture gains: the price of a unit of intelligence has fallen about thirteenfold a year since GPT-3 and about 47% a quarter at fixed capability; fast followers and distillation commoditize the frontier within months (open models lag by about four months); a commodity token ends up priced at the compute cost; Chinese labs can publish cheap open-weight models because their state is not answerable to a 401(k) class, so the US commercial frontier premium becomes a visible spread over the Chinese benchmark under permanent customer audit; trillions of capex cannot be repaid in twenty-dollar subscriptions; and competition forces labs and hyperscalers to keep spending as returns fall, destroying capital in aggregate. Its inverted thesis is that intelligence is the giveaway, a loss leader, and margins come from being the conduit; nothing that depends on model pricing margins escapes Genesis. Caveats it gives: frontier tokens stay worth far more than commodity ones; US inference margins are positive for now; Genesis revenue will keep growing; in its end state the lab splits into a commercial company that meters intelligence at whatever margin the Chinese floor allows and a sovereign frontier run cost-plus. Chips are the current crossing for a few more years, but not much longer. The paper does not discuss per-seat software vendors by name; it says firms will push the cost of wages and applications toward the cost of compute and shrink to a few operators.
